To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the civic competence of youth is higher in countries with high levels of democracy and economic prosperity, and where education systems are based on a liberal tradition.

1) The Nordic countries are the most successful in developing civic competence in young people; and 2) The Nordic countries have the highest levels of social justice and equality values and the lowest levels of ethnic and nationalist values.

the Nordic countries are the top performers in terms of civic competence, followed by the countries of the former communist bloc, and that the Southern and Eastern European countries perform the worst.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a new composite indicator of civic competence of youth in Europe and the identification of the most successful educational systems in the promotion of citizenship values and competences.
the question of how to measure and compare the civic competence of young citizens in Europe.

the question of whether there is a 'best practice' model of civic education in Europe or rather whether there are a number of different models of citizenship education that are equally valid in different national and cultural settings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Nordic countries' education system is most effective in developing critical thinking and values of equality but less successful in enhancing participatory citizenship attitudes and concepts of a good citizenship.
the Nordic approach to citizenship education, which is based on critical and autonomous thinking and a cosmopolitan perspective, is not the most fruitful approach for all aspects of citizenship.
the Nordic model of education is the most successful model in promoting the cognitive dimensions of citizenship but the Italian model is more successful in promoting the affective dimensions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the civic competence of young citizens in the European countries studied here is strongly related to the political and economic stability of a country and the extent to which the education system promotes autonomous critical thinking.
the Nordic countries are the most effective in developing the cognitive skills of citizenship and civic responsibility but are not the best in promoting participatory attitudes.

a liberal approach to citizenship education is the most effective in the Nordic system, a civic republican tradition in Italy and a critical/cosmopolitical approach in some of the former communist countries.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Nordic model of citizenship education is not necessarily the best for developing participatory citizenship.

the Nordic approach to citizenship education may facilitate the development of critical thinking and the values of social justice and equality but may not facilitate the participatory and civic attitudes and concepts of a good citizens which may be better facilitated by the civic republican and civic responsibility approach of the Italian teachers.

the measurement model of the civic competence of young Europeans can be used to monitor the impact of different education policies on the development of citizenship in the different national contexts.
